items.followUp: What occurs during the S phase of the cell cycle?

rubric.why: Identifies where G2 occurs in the cell cycle.
rubric.description: G2 is the second gap phase, occurring after DNA replication and before mitosis.
rubric.how: Award for correctly placing G2 after S phase and before mitosis.

rubric.why: States a main activity or function of G2.
rubric.description: During G2, the cell grows and makes proteins and other materials needed for mitosis.
rubric.how: Award for describing cell growth or the production of materials needed for mitosis.

modelAnswer: G2 is the second gap phase; it occurs after DNA replication (S phase) and before mitosis.
During G2, the cell grows and makes proteins and other materials needed for mitosis.

items.followUp: What is the function of photosystems in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Explains what photosystems are or what they do.
rubric.description: Photosystems are groups of pigment molecules and proteins that absorb light energy.
rubric.how: Award for identifying photosystems as pigment-protein groups or stating that they absorb light.

rubric.description: Photosystems are located in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
rubric.how: Award for locating photosystems in the thylakoid membrane(s) of chloroplasts.

modelAnswer: Photosystems are groups of pigment molecules and proteins that absorb light energy.
They are located in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.

items.followUp: Name two Muslim scientists and describe one scientific contribution of each.

rubric.why: Recognises a Muslim scientist and his contribution.
rubric.description: Jabir bin Hayyan made important contributions to chemistry.
rubric.how: Award for naming Jabir bin Hayyan and associating him with chemistry.

rubric.why: Credits a Muslim scientist with work on animals.
rubric.description: Al-Jahiz studied animals and wrote Kitab al-Hayawan.
rubric.how: Award for naming Al-Jahiz and identifying his zoological work or book.

rubric.why: Credits a Muslim scientist with work on plants.
rubric.description: Al-Dinawari contributed to botany and wrote Kitab al-Nabat.
rubric.how: Award for naming Al-Dinawari and identifying his botanical work or book.

rubric.why: Recognises a Muslim scientist and his medical contribution.
rubric.description: Ibn Sina was a renowned physician and wrote Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb.
rubric.how: Award for naming Ibn Sina and associating him with medicine or his medical text.

modelAnswer: Jabir bin Hayyan made important contributions to chemistry.
Al-Jahiz studied animals and wrote Kitab al-Hayawan.
Al-Dinawari contributed to botany and wrote Kitab al-Nabat.
Ibn Sina was a renowned physician and wrote Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb.

items.followUp: Compare the main characteristics of Kingdom Fungi and Kingdom Plantae.

rubric.why: States the defining cellular organisation of Monera.
rubric.description: Monerans are prokaryotic and lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for identifying Monera as prokaryotic or stating that it lacks a true nucleus.

rubric.why: Gives a characteristic or example of Monera.
rubric.description: Monerans are unicellular; bacteria and cyanobacteria are examples.
rubric.how: Award for giving a suitable characteristic or example of Monera.

rubric.why: States the defining cellular organisation of Protista.
rubric.description: Protists are eukaryotic and possess a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.how: Award for identifying Protista as eukaryotic or stating that it has a true nucleus.

rubric.why: Gives a characteristic or example of Protista.
rubric.description: Protista consists mainly of unicellular eukaryotes; Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena are examples.
rubric.how: Award for giving a suitable characteristic or example of Protista.

modelAnswer: Kingdom Monera consists of unicellular prokaryotes; they lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Bacteria and cyanobacteria are examples of Monera.
Kingdom Protista consists mainly of unicellular eukaryotes; their cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena are examples of Protista.

items.followUp: Describe how light energy is converted into chemical energy during the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Explains the role of chlorophyll and light in starting the reaction.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, exciting electrons to a higher energy level.
rubric.how: Award for stating that chlorophyll absorbs light or that light excites electrons.

rubric.why: Describes transfer of excited electrons through the light reactions.
rubric.description: Excited electrons pass along electron carriers in the thylakoid membrane.
rubric.how: Award for describing electron transfer through carriers or an electron transport chain.

rubric.why: Describes formation of the gradient used to make ATP.
rubric.description: Electron transport helps build a proton (H⁺) gradient across the thylakoid membrane.
rubric.how: Award for identifying a proton/H⁺ gradient across the thylakoid membrane.

rubric.why: Identifies how the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis.
rubric.description: Protons flow through ATP synthase, providing energy for ATP formation.
rubric.how: Award for linking proton flow through ATP synthase with ATP synthesis.

rubric.why: Gives the ATP synthesis reaction or names the process.
rubric.description: ATP synthase combines ADP with inorganic phosphate (Pi) to form ATP; this is photophosphorylation.
rubric.how: Award for stating that ADP and phosphate form ATP or naming photophosphorylation.

modelAnswer: Yes. Light and chlorophyll are essential for ATP synthesis in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which excites electrons to a higher energy level.
The excited electrons pass through electron carriers in the thylakoid membrane; their energy helps build a proton (H⁺) gradient.
Protons flow back through ATP synthase, providing energy for ATP formation.
ATP synthase combines ADP with inorganic phosphate (Pi) to form ATP; this process is called photophosphorylation.
